finding.claim: With caching enabled, a verified token that has no numeric `iat` claim is cached for the full `cacheTTL` (default 600000 ms) and its `exp`/`nbf` are ignored. A token whose exp has passed is still returned as valid from the cache. The exp-based cache expiry is only computed inside `if (hasIat)`. Otherwise `cacheValue[2]` stays 0 and is set to `clockTimestamp + clockTolerance + cacheTTL` at line 134.
finding.source: A signed token with `exp` but no `iat`, for example one issued with `noTimestamp: true` or by a third-party issuer. The attacker is anyone holding such a token, such as a stolen or leaked one, who replays it after it expires. Preconditions: the verifier has `cache` enabled, and the same token was successfully verified at least once before its exp, so a cache entry exists.
finding.sink: Cache hit branch in `verify()` (src/verifier.js:364-377) returns the cached payload as valid via `handleCachedResult`, skipping `verifyToken` and so skipping the `exp` and `nbf` validators.

trace.note: First successful verification calls cacheSet with the payload
hasIat is false when payload.iat is not a number, so the block that derives the entry's time range from nbf/exp (lines 119-130) is skipped
cacheValue[2] is 0, so it is set to maxTTL (now + tolerance + cacheTTL). The token's real exp is never considered
A later request with the same token finds [value,0,max]. min===0 and now<=max, so it is a cache hit
The cached payload is returned without re-running exp/nbf validation, even though exp has passed

finding.guards_checked: The cache hit condition checks only `min`/`max`, and both are derived by cacheSet. `exp` is not re-validated on a hit. The `hasIat` gate at line 117 is the only path that incorporates exp/nbf into the entry's lifetime. `maxAge` is also only applied inside that gate. The default cacheTTL is 10 minutes, so the exposure window is bounded by cacheTTL. The signature is checked on first verification, so this cannot be exploited without a validly signed token.
